[I have value $40. With five bidders and a third-price rule, bidding my true value balances winning competitive auctions while avoiding overpaying (the winner pays the third-highest bid). There is no history to exploit, values redraw independently, and overbidding risks paying above my value. A straightforward, near-optimal choice in this setting is to bid my value, which wins when I am the highest and yields positive surplus on average.]

[One round, no history. In a third-price auction with five bidders, bidders are incentivized to bid above value, but overbidding can cause payment (third-highest bid) to exceed my true value and produce losses. With no info on opponents' strategies and a single draw, I prioritize guaranteeing nonnegative payoff when I win. Bidding my true value ($32) avoids paying more than my value while still allowing me to win when others' bids are lower, maximizing expected profit conservatively given the uncertainty.]

[No past data. In a 5-bidder third-price auction the symmetric linear equilibrium solves b(v)=k v with k=4/3. So bid (4/3)*v. For v=$28 this gives $37.333..., round to the nearest $0.1. This strategy maximizes expected payoff under IID uniform values in repeated play.]

[With five bidders and a third-price (k=3) rule, the symmetric equilibrium for uniform values is b(v) = (n-1)/(n-k+1) * v. For n=5, k=3 this gives b(v)=4/3 * v. That exploits the cheaper payment rule while avoiding excessive overbidding. With my value $21, bid 4/3*21 = $28. ]
